utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution. For a moment I had forgotten who I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As long as you don't forget where you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Igor Pantelic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you asked us yesterday at the close of business to address you this morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- in relation to the Prosecution's notice in the particular Exhibits P1755 and P1756, and Your Honours will have seen that in paragraphs 5 through 7 of the Prosecution's notice they acknowledge several discrepancies between those two proposed exhibits. Your Honours will recall, having looked at that submission, that Mr. -- General Milovanovic did not review a complete version of P1755. He never reviewed P1756, and I'm referring to out-of-court review. And in court he reviewed only selected pages of P1756. The Prosecution also acknowledges discrepancies in that one document or one version of this document contains documents inserted into the book that are not in the other. We say that these discrepancies are significant. And I suppose we could ignore the elephant in the room, but I say we shouldn't. There are problems with these documents that we've raised with you in the past, and there is no rational basis on which to decide which of these two is authentic and ought to be admitted. But I'll take that point no further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Is there a response?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, obviously we don't agree. Mr. Hannis set out the major difference is the way that the documents were scanned. There is actually no problem with this; if Your Honours want it, the originals can come in to court and can be examined. So it's the originals which are the evidence, in effect. We are simply saying rather than bring them into court and have -- because it will cause problems with other cases, and have them made exhibits in this case, we want the scans. Mr. Hannis explained the difference; the only real difference is the scanning. As it was pointed out by Mr. Hannis, the general in fact in court identified the handwriting. And as I say, Your Honours, I don't know whether this is reopening the whole question of the admissibility of these documents as witnesses [sic]. If so, then obviously, as I say, we can call a great deal of further evidence about it. But Your Honours have accepted it. Mr. Hannis has given the explanation for the differences. And we invite Your Honours to simply admit or, rather, remove the MFI status from the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Well, it occurred to the Chamber, when we first saw Mr. Hannis's report with his candid observations about the apparent discrepancies, that they were matters which, notwithstanding the decision which the Chamber has already made and which it doesn't intend to revisit about the admissibility of these documents, that the -- in fairness, the Defence should have an opportunity to comment on it. And the -- but on a closer inspection, it appears to the Chamber that the discrepancies are not as stark as they may appear at a casual reading. And reminding all the parties that the question of weight of these documents has yet to be determined and will be a factor in the final resolution of this matter, we at this stage order that the MFI status of the documents be removed and they be marked as full exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: By way of clarification, it is the coloured versions which are being -- in respect of which the MFI status is being removed, and the black and white versions are not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I just return to something Your Honours just said, saying that it's a question of the weight. We understood the documents were admitted on the basis that Your Honours were satisfied these were authentic. If you're not so satisfied, then you couldn't have admitted them. The weight is a different matter in the sense of how much does it assist Your Honours in deciding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we aren't saying anything different, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I just was a little concerned when -- because you allied it with the question of the -- potentially the -- whether these documents were authentic or not because of the discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thought that had long been decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And to the extent that we can import the decision in Seselj as to the handwriting, from the handwriting expert, yes, we -- that adds weight to the decision that we have made in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, that's a little -- I think -- but may I say, out of caution, that's a little difficult because we haven't put the evidence in, in this case; we merely asserted yesterday that there was this evidence available if Your Honours needed to hear further evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I did say to the extent that we can import. So if there is nothing further, could we have the witness return to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown. Before Mr. Zecevic resumes his cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Now, as a matter of curiosity, Mr. Zecevic, your time estimate, does it still hold, in terms of what you had indicated yesterday? I mean before we started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I estimated five hours, but that was well before the direct examination. I will be able, at the -- probably at the second break to give you an indication whether I would be needing some additional time or not. At this point, I'm truly sorry but I can't give any estimate. I would hope to finish by end of today, but it's very likely that I will spill over to tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You said additional; I was thinking of reduction. But please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, yesterday we spoke about the laws and regulations which, in my opinion, and you agreed, are important for the understanding of the matters you dealt with in your expert report. You certainly have reviewed the Law on All People's Defence, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I have, although it was some time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact that from the aspects of doctrine and strategy of the armed forces of former Yugoslavia, that law was one of the most important because as it deals with the concept of all people's war to the minutest detail; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a law that clearly dealt with the Yugoslavian view on how the country was to act in a state of war or imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree. It's a fact also, isn't it, that in the Law on All People's Defence, and later we will also see that it also applies to the strategy which is a document that elaborates this matter, many issues that you dealt with in your expert report are contained, such as Crisis Staffs, the Territorial Defence, commanding the TO, leading the TO, volunteers, and the like. All these are explained and defined. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do. I'm not sure if - I now would have to review it - but whether Crisis Staffs are the words or phrases that they use. But from what I remember, the law regulates the Territorial Defence, the army, and also I think they often call them sociopolitical communes or organisations at local or regional level, as well as the League of Communists, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the law was adopted in 1982. At that time, the only political party on the territory of the former Yugoslavia was the Communist Party. And I agree with you that the law doesn't mention Crisis Staffs but committees for All People's Defence and social self-protection. I believe that is what you meant; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But those committees basically are the same thing. Although in 1992 they were called Crisis Staffs, they were actually the same thing as these bodies which in 1992 existed in the field and about which you speak in your report; correct? I mean as far as powers, structure, and their role go.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I would have to review all those bits and details, but I would agree generally that there was a structure in All People's Defence which was about mutual cooperation in all the fields. All People's Defence was a mechanism by which federal republic and local or municipal organs were to have a role in the defence of the country. And at local level or regional level, there were secretariats for National Defence, there were civil protection issues, there were civilian bodies that were meant to have function in assisting in the defence of the territory, along with the Territorial Defence and the JNA -- or the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will read out a section of text to you. Document 1D00-4042, tab 3, Article 74. And the page is 11 or 12, I believe, in Serbian, and I believe it's page 43 in English. Article 74.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] if we can get Article 74 on the screen, please. That's on page 12 in the Serbian text. And in the English translation, I believe it's page 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This Article refers to -- or, rather, it refers to Article 72, which lays out which bodies exercise command and control over the institutions of All People's Defence and social self-protection. And you will see here, halfway through the first paragraph, first it says: "If the competent organs mentioned in Article 72 are unable to discharge their tasks and duties, committees for All People's Defence and social self-protection shall carry out activities and measures in order to make these organs capable of continuing their work, and they shall mobilise the resources of All People's Defence, et cetera, until the appropriate organs are able to discharge their tasks and duties." This means, effectively, that command and control over the bodies of All People's Defence are in the exclusive remit of these competent organs, isn't it, sir? In a specific municipality.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it possible to look at Article 72 to talk about what the competent organs they're referring to are? I'm assuming that means the military or the TO, but is it possible to look at Article 72?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. That would be the previous page. There's a reference to Article 72, paragraph 1, the first paragraph of that article. I needn't read it out to you. You can read it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: And could you move back to Article 74 again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have Article 74.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's rather a lengthy article, both of them, but I read this as saying that in relation to -- bearing in mind the topic is to do with organs of local national defence, if they -- if the organs referenced in 72 are unable to fulfill their function, these are taken on by the committees for All People's Defence, which I'm assuming were the localised individuals who worked at municipal or local level to assist in the mobilisation, provide logistic support, and the likes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Article 74 says, in the second sentence that I have already read out to you but I will do so again: "If the competent organs mentioned in Article 72, paragraph 1, of this law are unable to discharge their tasks and duties, committees for All People's Defence and social self-protection shall ..." And then the last sentence: "... shall mobilise the resources of All People's Defence and social self-protection in their area and direct them until the appropriate organs are able to discharge their tasks and duties." This means, sir, that these committees mobilise all forces of All People's Defence, issue orders to them, carry out activities, and so on. That's what it means, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, it may mean that, if the competent organs referenced in 72 don't fulfil their function. And I'm assuming that this cuts to this issue of, you know, everyone had a function or a role within all Yugoslav -- All People's Defence. And if the localised organs of authority were unable to function, then the committees for All People's Defences would be empowered to take over that responsibility, which could include the issue of mobilisation or other issues like logistic support or cooperation. That's how I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree that all of this has been encompassed. However, this particular regulation is unambiguous and it envisaged exactly what their legislators had in mind. But let us not waste any more time on this issue. I'm going to show you now Article 104. And just for reference, on the same page you can see Article 75, which says that National Defence committees are responsible for their work to the organs that had set them up. In other words, if we are talking about a municipality, that would be the Municipal Assembly. Now, back to Article 104, on page 18 in Serbian and page 67 in English. Mr. Brown, I don't know if you had an opportunity or if you were interested at all in these matters, but Article 104 explains the notion of resubordination of militia or police in accordance with the law. This is something you discussed with Ms. Korner on the first day of your testimony. And it says that the police may be used for carrying out combat operations during which time the police shall be subordinated to the commanding officer. And it says, at the end, the reserve police -- forces of the police shall be reinforced by military conscript. Did you have an occasion to take a look at this article?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't looked at it recently, but I obviously read it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that in the event of an imminent threat of war and other emergencies, units of the TO may carry out work relating to maintaining public law and order, be engaged to fight terrorists and other sabotage forces, and carrying out other tasks relating to social self-protection? TO units shall be engaged in these tasks when they cannot be carried out by the internal affairs organs in a timely and effective manner. I have read this from the strategy of All People's Defence and social self-protection. For reference, that's page 58 in document 1D00526. I think it's under tab 4. What I've just read to you is on page 58, which is 31 in e-court in the Serbian and page 5 in the English. Now, the essence is that TO units, during an imminent threat of war and other emergencies, is entitled, under the law and these strategies, to act as if they were members of the Ministry of the Interior. Were you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't a part of my report to look at that particular issue. And I don't know if you're referencing the Law on All People's Defence or a different --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am reading this portion from the strategy of All People's Defence, which is a document, an official document, published by the Presidency on the 20th of May, 1987. And in its preamble it says that this strategy shall be implemented from the date of its coming into force. And it is an integral part and provides a better understanding of the law that we are talking about. So this regulation, as well, was in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now I see that Ms. Korner is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've just got a query. Your Honours, this document has not been fully translated, and it may be for obvious reasons, because it's a huge document, but the paragraph that Mr. Zecevic has just referred Mr. Brown to appears, as it were, in isolation. I have no idea what the preceding or succeeding paragraph is about. I would ask that we can have a translation giving the context of all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we asked the CLSS to translate the entire document at the very beginning, i.e., in September two years ago when we started these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, the documents was returned to us and we were instructed to highlight the relevant portions of the document which will then be translated. We were told that it was impossible to have the entire document translated. Now, I have to say that I am more than surprised that the OTP to date has not obtained such a significant document in English. It is almost incomprehensible that despite all the cases that we had before nobody thought it would be well-advised to have it translated. However, if we gain support from the Trial Chamber and from the OTP as well, we are going to reiterate our request to the CLSS to have this crucial document translated. And it is extremely important for understanding the Law on All People's Defence. For that reasons, I think that it must be translated in its entirety, but that means that, as I said, we would need support from the Trial Chamber due to the fact that we were denied the request to have the whole book translated. Or perhaps Ms. Korner may, with her associates and co-workers, select certain portions that she deems worthy of translation and then we'll do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, it's no good Mr. Zecevic trying to blame the OTP for his own shortcomings on this. My complaint is that this document has taken one paragraph in isolation, as we can see, and we have no idea what the context is. And Mr. Zecevic wants to make certain assertions to the witness based on a paragraph taken out of context. If he wanted to use it, then it was his obligation, not the OTP's, to make sure that a proper translation of such sections, not just paragraphs, was obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I have heard what counsel on both sides have said. And it seems to me that the practical solution to this problem, given the limitations which CLSS obviously has and notwithstanding the inevitable differences that would arise in adversarial proceedings in this context, one side may think that certain parts are necessary and the other side other parts, wouldn't the -- a way, and I understand Mr. Zecevic's explanation to Ms. Korner's last comment is that it was at the invitation of CLSS that the portions were highlighted which they were able to accommodate the translation of. So I'm wondering whether it is not possible, and perhaps I'm being terribly naive here but that's the prerogative of judges, for counsel, out of court, to agree portions of the -- this voluminous work, that would include in this case the paragraph now in contention, and arrange to have those translated into one of the working languages of the Tribunal. As I sit here, I see no alternative, but I'm willing to hear counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's all very well, but what my complaint is that they've picked a paragraph, it may well be that the rest of it supports their contention but I simply don't know that and nor does anybody else. And this is not a proper way, to just take a paragraph out, even with the complaint of CLSS. Your Honours, I don't want to waste any more time on this. I'm certainly going to say that this document, in its present translated form, cannot form part of any law library or whatever. I think it is coming out of the law library.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely the fact, that's the strategy of the All People's Defence is a part of law library, and it's been stipulated by the parties. And that's why I'm so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I certainly didn't, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Surprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I certainly didn't appreciate that what was being put into a law library was an annotated, apparently annotated by the Defence, version of the document, not even the original document is in the law library.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that's -- that's -- that's completely --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, why is this one out?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's completely incorrect, Ms. Korner. The whole document is a part of the law library. The whole document is a part of the law library in its original form. The problem that we have is that we have to approach, we have to ask, the CLSS to translate. If they say, No, we are not translating the whole document, please mark the parts where you think are relevant, and that is what we will translate; that's what we did. There was no other way for us. The Prosecution has their own translation department, and I would have hoped that, as I said, that the Prosecution has the -- at least the draft translation of the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, I don't think that this matter can be resolved at this stage. And what I would suggest is that, Mr. Zecevic, you proceed, and the -- at some point, Ms. -- the Prosecution may be in a position to challenge the context of the relevant passage to which you're referring the witness. But at this point it seems as if we aren't going to make any progress by arguing the methods any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but, Your Honour, I don't know I'm challenging the context or not because I don't know what the context is. I'm simply pointing out, and may I say that if I had realised that the law library, whether it's an annotated or an unannotated version, did not contain a proper translation, then I wouldn't have agreed. And I'm afraid we're going to have to go back over the law library and see what else hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's possible. But for the moment what I would suggest is that you flag this particular paragraph and see where you stand by the time -- when the time comes for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this gives me a grave concern. We spent more than six months agreeing on the law library, and it was a joint effort by both parties, and we jointly filed the law library documents with all its -- with all the documents in. And that was throughout the whole Prosecutor's case and according to the instruction of the Trial Chamber, and my understanding that we are going to stipulate to that, we didn't insist that any of the documents would be -- would be admitted as the exhibit. Now, if Ms. Korner -- if I understand right that Ms. Korner is going to revisit that, then we are just -- this is just not acceptable for us because then we will have to -- to return to point one and then ask all the documents to be admitted because we intend to rely on those documents. And based --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might interrupt, Mr. Zecevic. The concern that you are now articulating is something which would occur to everyone in the Court, including the Chamber, but, again, it is not something that can be resolved at this moment. And we are now all alerted that it may be something to which we will have to return at some -- at some point in the future, but let's proceed with the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just on that note say the rule is, and it may be we weren't thorough enough in checking, that a document which is admitted has to be in one of the working languages of the Tribunal. Now, I imagine that a cursory check was done and nobody appreciated certainly that this document was only partially translated. Because the front page has been translated, and all the rest of it ... and that's the problem. That's why I say it will have to be revisited. I mean, as a matter of strict rules, there has to be a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go any further. I would just state that we have at least 20 documents which were produced by the Office of the Prosecutor which have only partial translation and were admitted in this case. But let me move on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in this very same document, just for the sake of confirming what Ms. Korner has raised as a problem, if you look at page 151, that's in the book, whereas it's page 77 in e-court, page 12 in the English, it reads that in introducing and maintaining public law and order and carrying out other tasks of social self-protection, TO units enjoy all the powers as those enjoyed by the organs of the Interior. This is in the section entitled, "Engagement of Armed Forces in Emergencies." I presume that you are not familiar with this section either. You haven't read this part of the document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen any of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, let me ask you, then, the following: I'd like to clarify three principal questions with you. In your report, item 1.83 to 1.100, you speak about responsibilities of a unit; that was under tab 64 of the OTP which contained a map of a unit AOR, which is 65 ter 10639. So tab 64 in the OTP binder. That's the footnote of your item 143. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, tell me please, very briefly, how do you understand the term "area of responsibility" of a specific unit?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an area of responsibility is a zone or a piece of terrain set by a commander that that military unit is responsible for, in terms of its conduct and operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me, please, the fact is that it is incumbent on lower-ranking units to report regularly to higher-ranking units in all armies in the world, which naturally included the 1st Krajina Corps in 1992; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a recognised principle that lower formations report to higher ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And at least in the case of the VRS and before that in the JNA those were dubbed daily combat reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes they're called regular combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of such daily combat reports, let's say that 343rd Motorised Brigade from Prijedor sent daily reports to the 1st Krajina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume so. I haven't seen, for example, the archive of the 343rd Brigade, so I can't say that -- how often they sent them. But I would assume that as the corps itself wrote daily combat reports, that it was receiving similar reports from subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, since the 1st Krajina Corps sent their own daily reports to the Main Staff of the VRS, originally that was the command of the 2nd Military District at the time of the JNA and then it became the General Staff of the VRS, they compiled these daily reports on the basis of the daily reports collected from their subordinate units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would assume so. It may well have been that some of these reports were through telephone communications or meetings. But, you know, not having seen the archive of subordinate units, I can't say exactly. But it's clear that information was coming from subordinate units to the corps which was then compiling its own regular combat report which it forwarded to the Main Staff, or, as you say, in the day of the JNA, the 5th Corps would report to the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my third question: Yesterday, you will remember that we spoke at the beginning about combat tasks. Now, within a combat action, each task that is assigned within this action is actually a combat task; is that true?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. If a unit in the course of carrying out an offensive attack, one of the lesser units is tasked with guarding a road or whatever, could that be described as a combat task?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The phrase -- normally in combat operations, there are multiple actors. There clearly will be potentially fighting formations, infantry units or armour or artillery, but usually in combat operations there are many other support functions. These could be logistics, medical, police, military police issues, so it's not the case that what I understand to be, when we are referencing combat operations, that it means exclusively the forceful end of combat tasks. Usually, in military operations, in the planning phase, as I say, there are multiple actors who have roles in order to assist in the completion of combat operation. So it's not always the case that many of these actors -- and, in fact, from my knowledge, most of the actors involved in combat operations tend to be in a supporting function. So it may well be in your example where you say a lesser unit is tasked with guarding a road, that it may not be involved in combat operations, i.e., the fighting component at all, but that its function of guarding that road may assist in the -- in the end result, which could be allowing logistic supplies to securely traverse an area; it could be assisting in securing a road that was to be used for medical evacuation; it could be used to protect the road that could assist in the evacuation of prisoners. So my point is that combat operations do not just involve those who are firing weapons or weapon systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the essence of a combat task is that it opens up a possibility for an individual or a unit to come in close contact with the enemy, to exchange fire, and that what makes it a combat task. That's the difference. Because it allows for a possibility of exchanging fire with the enemy. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would generally agree with you. But that doesn't mean to say that everybody involved in the combat task is likely to -- to be involved in that exchange of fire or it would expect to. My point is that multiple actors can be involved in what are generally called combat operations, without the exchange of fire, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question: You are aware that the concept of the Yugoslav People's Army, as well as the concept of the Army of Republika Srpska, were both based on the unity and singleness of command. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the first day of your testimony, Ms. Korner showed you one of the directives. A directive is, as it were, an order of the highest level, because usually it comes from the General Staff of an army. This is how the sequence of order is established.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- some armies don't phrase it as a directive. But in terms of the VRS, it was -- they were called directives. They came through the Main Staff. And General Mladic or, I believe, in the case of some of the directives, Dr. Karadzic signed them. So yes they came from the highest organs of the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the first day of your testimony you looked at a document P1779, tab 58, that's the Prosecution document, and you spoke at the page 18658 to 18663 of the transcript about it. And the document in question is a more detailed working-out of the fourth directive that you also mentioned, that is, P1780; is that correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will certainly agree with me that every directive has to be put in a certain context, bearing in mind the time that it was created in, especially when we think about the particular order that the unit is supposed to execute in a certain area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document now, but I would like you to confirm that this document, P1779 and P1780, could you confirm that they date from the November 1992, the directive and also the more detailed working-out of that directive in the Zvornik Light Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, are you going to show me a document? I'm unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't my intention because I think that you have it at hand. It's tab 58. 1779. I would simply like us -- like us to place this into a context. It's basically a document that dates from the end of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Drina Corps command document you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And also the directive number 4, P1780; it also dates from November 1992 -- end of November?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to show you a document that, in my opinion, explains the reasons underlying the directive and also the part quoted by Ms. Korner. That's 1D04-9459, tab 153.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, Your Honours, can I ask is there a translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a combat order dated 30th of September, 1992, that the combat order issued by the commander of the armed forces of Srebrenica, Naser Oric, and some other commanders as well. This combat order is dated 30th of September, 1992. Have you had a chance to see this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen this document before. Do you want me to read the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you should take a look at the document during the break and then you could give your comments on it after the break. You shouldn't read the document now. It will be a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My associates will give you a copy through the usher.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like us to concentrate on a document that you analysed with Ms. Korner. It is tab 62; that's the Prosecution tab. P1781. That's the analysis of combat readiness and activities of VRS in 1992. That's something that you mentioned on the first day of your testimony, page 18664 of the transcript, up to and including 18686. And you said that this particular copy that you analysed and included in your report, and you also showed us to you during your testimony [as interpreted], that that is a copy obtained from the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that the -- there is no reason to doubt the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. It was within the wider collection of the documents that had been seized, I believe, from the corps headquarters prior to me joining the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since you quoted the document on a number of occasions in your report, I assume that it is rather relevant for your report, especially information contained therein.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it's a relevant document. I mean, it's not the only one, obviously, and it's one of many, but I do believe it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order to be very clear, I'm going to try to follow the methodology of Ms. Korner. You first spoke about page 10 in English, and page 11, concerning the two periods mentioned in the analysis, two periods in the development of the command and control in VRS.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's referenced in that -- sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that the page in English ought to be 10, and it's page 11 in Serbian, one page after this one. Now we have the correct page in Serbian, yes. I'm sorry, I was guided by the transcript, 18665. That's when you spoke about it. So the last paragraph in English. In its analysis, the Army of Republika Srpska divided its process of command and control into two periods: the first one from the 1st of April to the 15th of June, and the second period from the 15th of June onwards. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And here they say, the same page, that the first period is mostly characterised by self organisation on the municipal and on the regional units which then were transformed into municipal and other regional units based on the -- on the TO units. And you also spoke about this, it says that these units usually secured and liberated their municipalities and stopped at that. So in essence those units were self-organised and they had a very local character; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe they generally did. From my reading of the military documents, the Territorial Defence units weren't the only ones involved in that. Certainly in the Krajina Corps. I can't talk about other areas. But in the Krajina Corps, it wasn't just the Territorial Defence that was -- that was involved in that. Clearly, elements of the 5th Corps, 1st Krajina Corps, were engaged too. There had been announcements in April by the Serbian authorities to establish the Serb TO and to secure territory. So although the dates seem -- there is -- they reference the 15th of June, for example, yet the army was established on -- at the 16th Assembly Session on the 12th of May, and it's clear that the VRS were already functioning in that period between the 12th of May and the 15th of June. But in terms of a division, it would seem that that -- the characteristic is generally borne out by the documents that I have reviewed. Municipal authorities were involved in taking control of territory, it did involve, at times, Territorial Defence units, along with support from the VRS or the JNA. And then later, as they describe, there were more strategic operations. For example, you mention these directives. But the characterisation, I think, is reasonably accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify one thing here. I think that it is necessary to clarify the reasons because of which the army decided to divide this period in two. It is a fact, isn't it, that it was only on the 12th of May that the Assembly made a decision to establish the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they announced it on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Up until that point, there was JNA.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was the JNA and there was the Serbian Territorial Defence too. But there was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's also a fact that the JNA withdrew pursuant to an order from Bosnia-Herzegovina but only on the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of May there was an instruction in relation to the withdrawal of the JNA. However, in reality, what happened, although there may have been some withdrawals of strategic forces and some other issues, in reality, at least in the Krajina Corps, the JNA did not withdraw. The JNA was simply transformed into the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know that. But the essence here is that up until at least the 12th of May all orders, all directives, were issued by the organs based outside the territory of Republika Srpska. They were the JNA organs, it was -- then there was the Presidency of the SFRY and similar organs; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you talk about all orders and directives, were you talking about all orders and directives through the JNA, or are you talking about more widely than the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the military aspect. Until the 12th of May, the military could not possibly receive any order from Mr. Karadzic because the Army of Republika Srpska did not exist up until that moment. So it received the orders from the JNA and the Presidency, because the Presidency was the Supreme Commander. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- there was clearly a chain of command from the 1st -- the 5th Corps to the 2nd Military District, and they seemed to follow that. However, there were instructions in this prior period that the JNA or units of the 1st -- the 5th Corps were to establish communications with organs, and there clearly were links to the Serbian authorities prior to that. But formally, yes, I would agree with you that the chain of command from the 5th Corps ran through to the 2nd Military District, which I'm assuming then ran to the federal secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 13 of the same document, both in English and Serbian, we can find the clarification, the clarification of the initial situation from the 1st of April until the 15th of June, 1992. And it says here, the first paragraph, point 111: "The infantry units which, through self organisation, grew on a massive scale out of the Territorial Defence and other units were used only at the beginning of the war according to the decisions of Crisis Staffs and similar authoritative bodies." Sir, this is completely in line with what we said in the beginning when we were talking about the Law on All People's Defence; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is what it says in the document, but it -- and it would seem to be borne out in some municipalities that I observed that Crisis Staffs were heavily involved in -- in the process of securing territory at the municipal level. I wouldn't say that that was the only -- that the only way that infantry units were used. You know, the 43rd Motorised Brigade, if this is dealing with the -- or the 5th Kozara Brigade, for example, some of those were used, for example, in assisting in the taking over of power in Prijedor in -- at the end of April. So I wouldn't argue that it was only that, but it would seem to be that the Crisis Staffs in that early period did have a significant input into the taking of control of territory at municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm simply giving you comments of this analysis. I have no hidden agenda here. I'm not trying to establish something that is not contained in this document. I simply want to get your comments on this document. The second sentence: "Among the infantry units, there were also units which represented various political structures, which were sometimes in opposition to the overall objectives of our war. Some of them developed into 'paramilitary formations,'" in inverted commas. "These units mainly executed missions in the territories of their own municipalities or even in smaller areas. Initially, the units elected their own commanders." Now, when it says here that they elected their own commanders, it does contain a certain degree of mockery, this sentence, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to comment whether it's a mocking statement or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Surely you will agree with me that it is not possible to elect one's own commander. Commanders are always sent by orders. They are always appointed by a higher command.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally that would be the case. But clearly I think they are highlighting that at times this didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I entirely agree with you. And if you look at the following sentence, you can see: The target of actions were chosen collectively, and individuals or groups sometimes abandoned the set goals. When they say "chosen collectively," they are referring, obviously, to Crisis Staffs and other bodies which made such decisions, and then sometimes in execution of those orders, certain units would abandon the goals, or maybe even the Crisis Staffs themselves would abandon the goals. That's the conclusion that we can draw from here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- yeah, that would seem to be one of the conclusions that could be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm reminded about the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. If this is convenient, we are a couple of seconds short of 10.25. If this is a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break, to resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness makes his way back to the stand, we have a brief ruling to deliver. On 1 November 2010, the Prosecution filed confidentially its 17th motion for protective measures. In an oral ruling of 25 November, the Trial Chamber denied the motion without prejudice with regard to Witnesses 32 and 36. Subsequently on 9 December, the Prosecution filed confidentially a motion seeking reconsideration of the Trial Chamber's 25 November oral ruling. On 15 December, the Defence orally responded to this motion and stated that they took no position. The Trial Chamber notes that by denying, without prejudice, the Prosecution's motion of 1 November with regard to 32 and 36, it clearly opened the possibility for the Prosecution to file a new, well-founded motion for the protective measures initially denied. Therefore, it is procedurally unhelpful to reintroduce such a request by way of a reconsideration motion. Consequently, the Chamber will treat the Prosecution's motion as a supplemental motion and will disregard the arguments for reconsideration. The Trial Chamber notes that ST-032 and his family reside in the area where the alleged events described in his statement occurred. The Trial Chamber further notes the security incidents described in the newspaper article and the letter attached to the motion. The Chamber is satisfied that the fear expressed by this witness, should it become publicly known that he gave evidence before the Tribunal, has been established and has an objective foundation. Accordingly, the Chamber grants the Prosecution's request for a pseudonym for ST-032. The Trial Chamber is not satisfied that ST-036's fear has a strong objective foundation. Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber notes that while the witness no longer resides in the area where the events described in his statement occurred, he still has family there with whom he remains in close contact. The Chamber further notes that the witness is a victim and survivor of violence and that he declared to the Prosecution that he feels "extremely stressed whenever he receives calls from the ICTY which causes him to have to use medication." Furthermore, the Trial Chamber notes that having -- after having opposed the 1 November motion, the Defence did not take a position with regard to the 9 December motion. Having considered all the above, including the right of the accused to a fair trial and seeking to maintain a fair balance between the protection of victims and witnesses on the one hand and the right of the public to access information on the other, the Trial Chamber grants, in the interests of justice, the Prosecution's request for pseudonym for ST-036. The Trial Chamber also recalls its decision of 2 November in which it ordered the Registrar, after the Trial Chamber has ruled on the Prosecution's 17th motion for protective measures, to ensure that the evidence admitted is entered into the trial records in accordance with all protective measures in place and assign exhibit numbers to the statements, official transcripts, and associated exhibits admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, let us first finish what we were talking about concerning the analysis of combat readiness. Let us return to page 11 and be more specific about the second period. That can be found on page 10 in the English version in e-court. And this chapter reads that between the 3rd and the 19th May, the Main Staff of the VRS was constituted and that pursuant to a decision of the Presidency of the RS of 15 June about the organisation, establishment, and commanding of the VRS, the army started functioning, all pursuant to an order of the commander of the Main Staff of the 16th of June, which was -- which dealt with the implementation of the main objectives. You have already commented on that, so I believe we do not need to repeat that for the record, do we?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only that I think the decision of the Presidency of the 15th of June was probably -- I haven't seen a document relating to this, but it probably took some of the recommendations that had been requested of the various corps. And presumably some staff work or some work had been done in that period in early June to have the formal -- a formal document coming from the Presidency. But I think in my report I would argue that almost immediately after the 12th of May the VRS is functioning. General Talic clearly knows that he has to send reports up to the Main Staff. He's responding to mobilisation instructions. And the Directive 1, for example, was dated the first week -- or the 9th of June. So clearly work had been going on within the VRS Main Staff, and I think this date of the 15th of June is probably when a formal document was written. At least that's my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 18655 you deal with the interim period between the 12th of May and the 15th of June, and you said that there was a sort of lacuna or vacuum in that period, if I remember correctly. But objectively speaking, the army functioned, which isn't in dispute, by the way.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a vacuum, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I quoted you. That's what you said on page 18655. Let me check.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you say, 18665, line 21: "That doesn't mean to say that I think when this army was established on the 12th of May that they were not -- the Main Staff was somehow in vacuum, because there are, for example, the mobilisation instruction was passed on the 20th of May by Presidency, passed down through the Main Staff to General Talic."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He said they weren't in a vacuum, not they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff was somehow in a vacuum.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is what is written in the transcript. I believe all of us can read.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but I think it's ... he's saying: That doesn't mean to say that I think when this army was established on the 12th of May that the Main Staff was somehow in a vacuum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise if I misunderstood you. At any rate, sir, it is obvious that the army considered the period from the 1st of April to the 15th of June an irregular period in a way; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't describe it as that, and I don't think they describe it as that. I think the period is marked by a transition from the JNA into the VRS. That's how I would see it. And the initial establishment of the VRS components.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, it's a fact, isn't it, that up until 19 May -- and now I'm only referring to facts -- up until 19 May the JNA was present in Bosnia-Herzegovina; up until 12 May, there is no Assembly decision to establish the VRS; the army here speaks about units that organised themselves, that were commanded by commanders elected in a self-management-like way; and fourthly, a general mobilisation was only ordered on the 19th of May. The first directive is dated 9 June. These are all facts that you also mentioned in your -- in your document. And are you saying that all these facts do not point to the existence of a situation of irregularity?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I wouldn't necessarily say one way or the other whether they were regular. I agree with you those were the stated facts and those are the descriptions that are referenced in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, sir, 20 minutes ago you and I agreed that one of the basic principles upon which the organisation of the JNA and the VRS is founded was unity of command and singleness of command. These are the principles upon which both the JNA and the VRS were founded. So the period until -- roughly until the beginning of June is marked by the absence of these principles. There is -- there is no unity of command or singleness of command. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, within the JNA and the VRS, I would say there is. I would certainly agree that there are these other bodies; for example, the Serb TO, the mobilisation of the Serb TO in April and the involvement of the Serb TO as municipal level. But clearly, in that period, March, April and May, the JNA, at least in the Krajina Corps, are moving closer to the position of the SDS and are involved in cooperating with and assisting the TO, the Serb TO, and integrating those units into the newly established VRS. After all, General Talic himself orders his units, when he goes back -- when they go back to many of the municipalities, to establish cooperation and coordination with the authorities on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will speak about that later. Let us first comment that Directive 4, the document that I gave you for review during the break. You have reviewed the order issued by Naser Oric, dated 30 September 1992, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have briefly looked at it over the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Among others, on page -- just a moment. The document is 1D04-9459, tab 153. On page 4 of the Serbian text, and I assume that the page reference is the same for the English text, there is the decision passed by Naser Oric and it says: "We decided to attack the well-known Chetnik stronghold of Kravica with a brigade numbering 1500 fighters and destroy it completely." I suppose that this is not the right page. We need page 5 of the English translation. Or probably it is 6, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seven, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first sentence that I read out can be found here. You will certainly know that the village of Kravica was indeed attacked. This is a generally known event which occurred on Christmas day in January 1992, when Naser Oric's forces massacred the people in that Serb village. Do you -- are you -- do you know of that event?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area is not one that I know well. I would defer to someone else that does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And at the very end there is a comment or, rather, Naser Oric's conclusion. I suppose, that can be found on the following page of the document or possibly at the very bottom of this page, I believe it's the following page in English. You see that Naser Oric's conclusion and his instruction is that as many children as possible must be taken prisoner, who will then be exchanged on -- in line with the all-for-all principle. You will agree with me, sir, won't you, that this wartime order must be placed into the context of the directive and the tasks given to the Drina Brigade which we saw, and that is P1779. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept -- again, I don't know this area well and you mentioned a date of December and whether this is after the period -- after the directive, I'm not sure. But certainly the first part of the instruction seems to be dated prior to the directive, the RS directive; and the combat order, at least the first part of the combat order, at face value, seems to be an order instructing Muslim forces in that area who are surrounded to break out towards Tuzla in order to -- in order to allow refugees and the population who are not going to be mobilised and the wounded to move out, and, as part of that operation, to conduct a combat operation in a particular area. Again, I don't know the details at all, but if this occurred, it would seem to have set some, you know, be a part of the contextual chronology of the events in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us return to document P1771. That is the tab 62 in the Prosecution binder. We already commented on it. On page 18681 of your testimony on the first day, the Prosecutor read out to you a paragraph - on pages 45 and 46 in English, and in Serbian it's page 41 - about military and political meetings which the military says have taken place, and several meetings of the unit command and the local authorities are mentioned. Do you remember commenting on that? It's the following page in English. Paragraph 2.1.2. And the second paragraph in the text. It begins with, "Despite all the problems ..." I'm being warned that on page 35, 15, P1771 is mentioned, whereas I'm talking about document P1781. While the Prosecutor was reading this section to you, he -- she stopped off halfway through it. There is a sentence that reads: "A series of military and political consultations was held to consider the situation, course of combat operations, the functioning of political authorities and problems of cooperation between civil authorities and the army. Numerous joint actions were organised to harvest the crops, prepare and construct infrastructure facilities, procure fuel, and generally carry out preparations for winter, provide for refugees and the families of fighters killed and wounded in battle, and such like." Sir, when we spoke about your experience as a member of the British army yesterday, you said that as a member of the British army, you provided support or assistance upon the request of civilian authorities in Northern Ireland; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the overall military operation there was, in fact, characterised as support to the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it's a fact, isn't it, that as we have seen, and as you well know from the laws and regulations that you reviewed, that the JNA and the VRS consistently and greatly relied on the support of the civil -- civilian authorities and the people, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree with that. I mean, at the end of the day, the people are the ones who provide conscripts for the army. But more widely, yes, there is logistic issues, and funding was another issue. So I would accept that point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that, if I understand you properly, you and I agree that essentially there must be some sort of relationship between the army and the civilian authorities in an area; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe there was -- at least in the area that I looked at, there was within the VRS and the authorities in the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Further on in the commentary of this document, on page 72 of the document - that's 73 in English - the Prosecutor read to you an entry about the ethnic affiliation of the -- of professional officers serving in the VRS. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about that, during the examination-in-chief you spoke about removing non-Serb officers round about June 1992 from positions of authority in the VRS, or, to be more specific, at least in the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that's also contained in a small section in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, sir, isn't it, that the conflict in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to its main characteristics, was a civil war and that the parties to the conflict were basic -- were basically different in terms of ethnicity, that the parties were based almost exclusively on the ethnic principle; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if there's some legal issue in relation to civil war, but it would seem to me, at face value, that certainly was an internal conflict. Or maybe there was legal issues, whether it was external as well. But there was a civil war, yes, and the parties divided very much on ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you are not a legal expert, so I'm not insinuating anything of the kind. I'm merely focusing on that which you came to testify about as an expert. On page 78, and in English I believe it's page 86, which is in section 5.2, security measures. Under item 3, the security administration of the VRS speaks about a counter-intelligence assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's at the very beginning of the text. I don't believe that this is the correct page. Page 78, as far as I remember -- oh, yes, this is it. I apologise. So it was 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see here that the counter-intelligence assessment is to the effect that about 600 cases were identified in units in the territories of the RSK and the FRY and that this counter-intelligence assessment was not made for any unit of the VRS. They go on to list the reasons why, in their opinion, ethnic affiliation of the officers is a huge problem for the security of the units and for the -- and of the Army of Republika Srpska. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I -- is it paragraph 3 that's relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just take a second to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, would -- do you want me to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would just ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Undoubtedly then, not from the aspect of counter-intelligence, the ethnic affiliation of an officer in a high position in the VRS is a risk in terms of the possibility of leaking information from that position to the enemy. That is their assessment, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't read this per se dealing with that issue. I would accept that the VRS may view those in -- from a different ethnicity in a position of authority, that there is a risk there. I would accept that position. But I think this paragraph relates to the fact that they initially hadn't conducted counterintelligence assessments in units and when they did, that there were some cases which were highlighted. But they're more widely just -- than just the VRS. There clearly are individuals who may fall in the category of those from other national affiliations, but there are others who maybe have family relationships, there are others who -- members of other military intelligence organisations, so there's a number of categories, presumably. Out of all those categories, they have 600 cases which they are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But in any case, from the security point of view held by the army security organs, all these facts enumerated under item 3 constitute potential risks for the security of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would accept that that could be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it is also a fact, isn't it, that some officers, after they had left the active-duty service in the Yugoslav People's Army, led units, and even sometimes rebellious units, not to mention that in the armies on the opposite side they held command positions. I suppose that you are also aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't study the army, the Bosnian army. There was others who looked at that. I know that that is a reference in the Krajina Corps documents that they are very worried that not only that the individuals will go on to the other side. And I would assume that there were -- without knowing the details, I would assume that there were ex-JNA or ex-TO members in the ABiH. It would seem that that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, let me remind you that on the first day you confirmed to me that you attended the interviewing of, for example, Mr. Osman Selak. In his statement, he confirmed that while he was in the Army of Republika Srpska, at a position of responsibility, he concurrently provided information to the opposite side. After his active service was terminated, he became a resistance movement leader in Banja Luka, if I remember correctly his words. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time since I worked here --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have the actual page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the break I will provide the paragraph -- relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree; I just thought that you would have remembered this as something outstanding. Now, sir, from that point of view, the dismissal of non-Serb officers, in terms of how security organs thought, was something that was fully justified, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't necessarily agree that just because someone is from one ethnicity that that would mean that they have to be removed. I accept that there could be a risk and that risk might need to be managed, and it would seem that when this policy within the army of removing those non-Serb was implemented that it seemed to be echoed throughout other structures of the RS. So I wouldn't automatically say it was justified as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But in view of the context and the nature of the conflict that was going on in the former Yugoslavia and in light of the facts mentioned before, it has been confirmed without any doubt that certain officers of the 1st Krajina Corps, while they were discharging their duties, did things that were absolutely in contravention of both the law and the military ethics. Under such circumstances you would agree with me that their removal would have been fully justified, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the documents that I've seen, I don't think the non-Serbs in the military were removed on the basis of contravention of law and military ethics. I think there was a decision to put non -- and I'd to refresh myself on the documents, but there was a decision to put non-Serbs -- to send them back to Belgrade, have their service in essence terminated. And it wasn't -- at least from the documents anyway, it wasn't on the basis that they had broken the law or that they had done something wrong in terms of military ethics. Now, the reference in the analysis readiness report indicates that there has been investigations, intelligence investigations, to see if there are weaknesses or security risks within the corps. And they've highlighted a number of those. It doesn't say that they are senior officers, presumably it's corps-wide. Actually it's VRS-wide, I believe. So I don't think it's just the 1st Krajina Corps. So -- and those are risks that are being looked at, investigations ongoing. But in relation to the Krajina Corps, it's my belief that the non-Serb officers were sent back to Belgrade, they didn't come back, and it wasn't done because of any apparent investigation or breaches of the -- of military discipline or law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, but it might have been the case in individual instances. But basically the order that you mentioned and commented during -- in examination-in-chief was definitely inspired by the risk that the security administration is talking about.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I would argue that the timing of the removal of non-Serb officers from the 1st Krajina Corps is as much related, if not exclusively related, to the discussions that were going on at the regional level in the Krajina about having non-Serb officials in positions of authority. And it was clear that at the 12th -- or, sorry, the 16th Assembly Session, that this issue was being discussed, because Mladic is one of the, in fact, probably the only official there who says -- we talked about Colonel Hasotic -- he's the only one who's saying, No, there are reasons why we should have these people within the VRS. And one of those reasons he gives is that he would rather have them in the trenches fighting with them than in the trenches opposite fighting against him. But despite that, it's clear that within a matter of weeks Mladic himself pushes out an instruction saying that these individuals are to go to Belgrade and have their status assessed. And they certainly don't appear to come back to the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would most kindly ask you, Mr. Brown, because my time is limited, to focus and to give me direct answers. Whatever you have said in examination-in-chief is already on record. Therefore, kindly focus on my specific questions. Now, the last thing that I would like to discuss with you, vis-à-vis this report, is item 10 on page 80 in Serbian and page 90 in English. So item 10, which you commented on transcript page 18685. I have the third sentence specifically in mind here, and I think that my learned friend Ms. Korner also read it, and it says: "Cooperation with the MUP of Republika Srpska is not deemed very good due to the passivity of the organs and lack of their desire to cooperate with us." This is, again, the position that the security organs of the Army of Republika Srpska had taken; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's as it says, that clearly there are issues with cooperation. Obviously, they particularly point out cooperation with the RSK and Serbia and give an example of why what has happened when cooperation hasn't gone well. But I -- you know, I take it at face value that this is a reference that there needs to be areas of improvement in that area -- in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We are going to document this in our further examination. Now I'd like to move to the question of Crisis Staffs. You spoke about this under the chapter of cooperation between military and civilian authorities, that's 18685, and it starts at 18702 of your examination-in-chief. We both agreed on the nature of these Crisis Staffs as being similar to the committees for All People's Defence and social self-protection that were enshrined in the Law on All People's Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In respect, maybe not necessarily in those who are fulfilling the functions, but in terms of the All People's Defence there were civilian bodies at various levels that were to cooperate with the Territorial Defence, be involved in mobilisation, have a secretariat for National Defence, liaise with the JNA, and the likes; and these would seem to be similar to the Crisis Staffs in the documents that I observed in the Krajina. May well have been that all we did was to utilise that type of template.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you must know that the Crisis Staffs existed throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that all the conflicting parties -- all parties to the conflict had them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not aware of all the details, but I would -- I think I remember some references that colleagues had talked, so it wouldn't surprise me that there were Crisis Staffs in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, bearing that in mind, I was somewhat surprised by your comment under 1.103, where you talk about the Crisis Staffs and the role of the SDS in the formation of these Crisis Staffs. Now, are you aware that the first Crisis Staff that I managed to identify in this case was established by the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the document 1D108, tab 151. Sir, I don't know if you had an opportunity to see this document before. It's minutes of the meeting of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 21st September, 1991. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you are not aware of the Crisis Staff headed by Ejup Ganic being established by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't sir. The Crisis Staffs really were not the focus of my report, and I know that there were other colleagues in other analytical teams that were looking at the issue of Crisis Staffs. But I haven't seen this document before, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
