utterances.text: Thank you. In your work, you make reference to a government instruction, which is P70 of the OTP document, that -- your footnote 292, which is an extract of the instruction --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the details of the instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is an instruction or, rather, an excerpt from the instruction for the operation of the Serbian people in municipalities. It's dated the 26th of April, 1992, and it was signed by Prime Minister, Professor Dr. Branko Djeric. In other words, it's P70 document, OTP tab 3. You made reference to this instruction in your footnote 292; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that's correct. I know I do reference it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you specifically commented item 4 of this document, where it is explicitly stated that the command of TO and police forces shall exclusively be carried out by professional personnel, therefore any interference with the command and control of TO and the use of the police should be prevented at any cost. That was your comment; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that your comment in your report was that, in spite of that, there is evidence beyond any doubt that the Crisis Staffs, irrespective of what is said here, commanded the TO, issued instructions, and used the police force. And then you go on by citing a number of examples.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can you point me to the part of my report that says that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you please give me a moment. I rephrased what you said. I may be wrong. In paragraph 2.26, you have quoted this particular excerpt from Mr. Djeric's instruction, but then under item 2.28 you said it was not only the SDS or local Crisis Staffs that stressed the need for cooperation or attempted to control the TO in the period prior to its full integration into the VRS.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would stand by that comment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that the Government of Republika Srpska, as early as on the 23rd of May, 1992, adopted a conclusion and proposed measures to be introduced towards terminating the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, sir. I'm not an expert on Crisis Staffs. I know that the Crisis Staffs remained in existence past that date, from the documents that I've seen. And then there were instructions on the changing of Crisis Staffs into War Presidencies. But I don't know the full details of the operations of Crisis Staffs. I know that other analysts worked on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the reason I'm asking you this is not that you didn't deal with Crisis Staffs but, rather, this was prompted by your comment under items 1.107 to 8, under item 1.108 -- 7, you say that the Crisis Staffs were a major factor in the general pursuance of policies of the SDS and the functioning of the self-proclaimed Bosnian Serb organs on the ground. This is what you claim.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I would argue that from the documentation I've seen, that that would seem to be the case. We mentioned the analysis report; it also talks about the importance of the municipal organs. So I would stand by that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, item 1.108 contains the conclusion that I just made reference to a minute ago, and this is what you say: "Although it was not necessarily envisaged that the Crisis Staffs were to directly command or order military units into combat actions, especially as the military had their own recognised chain of command, at times, and in certain municipalities, the Crisis Staffs did pass instructions to the military to carry out certain combat activities." This is what's written here. Now, let us go back to 1.107. Sir, if I tell you, as I already did, that it was the government who requested the Crisis Staffs to be abolished way back on the 23rd of May, 1992, would that have altered any of the conclusions that you reached in your item 1.107? I can show you the document, that's P217, tab 155 of the Stanisic Defence team, item 4, which is the minutes of the meeting of the cabinet or the government of the 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see it if I'm meant to comment on that document. Oh, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's in front of you, sir.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 4.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't necessarily change at all the reference I have in my report. I mean, I think from item 4, they are -- appear to be discussing the establishment of War Presidencies, and I mentioned that there were Crisis Staffs and later on they were changed to War Presidencies. But as far as I'm aware, there was not much of a change in practicality. I don't think I would change the reference in my report that you allude to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that on the 31st of May a decision was taken to form War Presidencies, and this decision was amended on the 10th of June, when decision to set up war commissioners' office were -- was taken, and we are talking about considerably different organs from the Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. That's not a proper question. That's a matter of argument. It's not accepted. It's not evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I accept that, but I'm trying to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know that a decision was made on the 10th of June to set up wartime commissioners' offices?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was the government who appointed commissioners to these offices responsible for individual municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not part of my report, sir, and I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But bearing in mind that it is you who state that the Crisis Staffs were important and that you stand by that statement, you told me so when I gave you a chance to change your view, after you have been able to acquaint yourself with the documents that you hadn't reviewed before, so now I have to ask you: Why do you think that the Crisis Staffs were abolished and changed if they were so important, as important as you claim in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my report is not a report on the functionings of the Crisis Staffs. But it's clear to me that when the Crisis Staffs were in operation, that they were an important feature in seizing control of territory and a vehicle by which civilian police and military structures would function in order to take control of territory. And documents from Prijedor, documents from Kljuc, references from Sanski Most, some references from Kotor Varos would seem to bear that out. Now, I can only go back in saying that I'm not an expert on Crisis Staffs, so the chronology of Crisis Staffs and how they may have changed, I'm aware, as I said, that they established War Presidencies; but in terms of a full analysis of that or any other bodies, it was out -- it was out with the remit of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I accept your explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I concur with counsel Zecevic that we have to explain -- accept your explanation, but are you able to form an opinion about why the Crisis Staffs were replaced with the war commissions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may well have been that the Crisis Staffs had fulfilled their function. It may well have been that in a number of municipalities they'd done as they'd been expected, what had been expected of them. There might also be some chronology in relation to the establishment of Crisis Staffs and then the subsequent establishment of the VRS. The establishment of the Crisis Staffs, again, I'm not an expert on this, but there was a fairly protracted period, I believe, and, if you like, the formal establishment; it was still possibly unclear on exactly how the JNA was going to fit into the picture. And it may well have been that once that was resolved and the full establishment of the VRS and the integration of the TO, that might have had a different -- you know, the Serb authorities may have looked at it slightly different -- differently. But I do countenance all this that I am not an expert in the issue of Crisis Staffs, and I didn't study them in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, today, at the very beginning, I read to you certain passages from the Law on All People's Defence and we had some comments on that and we saw that in certain cases, those organs, the commissions for All People's Defence - I think it was Article 74 that we looked at - in case that competent authorities were unable to execute their functions, those local organs were supposed to execute All People's Defence, organise actions, and lead the defence in the territory. So this whole situation -- and we have also seen the report by the military, that they have divided it into two periods and said that the first period, up until the mid-June, they said that it was very chaotic, from April to June 1992. You are going to agree with that, based on all the documents that we have reviewed so far?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is your question about whether I think the situation was chaotic, or is your question about whether -- related to this issue of All People's Defence and the bodies taking control?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The first question is: Do you agree with me that the situation was chaotic?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it could be classified as that, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then if you bear that in mind, I claim that the reason that on the 23rd of May the decision was made to abolish the Crisis Staffs and then on the 31st to introduce War Presidencies and immediately after that, on the 10th of June, to introduce war commissioners' offices, the only reason for all that is the fact that the central authorities were attempting to organise and control governmental bodies in the territory, which was not the case up to that time.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would not agree with that position. I would argue that Crisis Staffs appeared, in the areas that I saw documentation, to do very much as had been expected of them in April, that these were not organisations or groups acting on their own, and that the establishment of Crisis Staffs by the Serbian authorities had been to take control of territory. And that's very much what they did. And the Crisis Staffs had a reporting chain, they weren't operating on their own, they had a reporting chain from the documentation that I have seen, for example, Kljuc municipality seemed to act on instructions that were passed down to them. It was a municipality where there was civilian TO and military involvement and police involvement. And I can't tell you why they may have wanted to change Crisis Staffs into War Presidencies or anything else, and it might have been an embryonic process of establishing the Bosnian Serb authorities, but I wouldn't say -- I wouldn't agree with your characterisation of Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, this is a convenient point to take the break, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness is brought in, please, can I just raise one matter. And it really -- the simple points is that when propositions are being put from other evidence, it must be put accurately. And Your Honour will have heard that I've objected on a number of occasions. At page 40 of today's transcript -- 40, yes, line 5, the question was put to Mr. Brown: "Mr. Brown, let me remind you that on the first day you confirmed to me that you attended the interviewing of, for example, Mr. Osman Selak. In his statement, he confirmed that while he was in the Army of Republika Srpska, at a position of responsibility, he concurrently provided information to the opposite side. "After his active service ... terminated, he became a resistance movement leader in Banja Luka, if I remember correctly his words. Are you aware of that?" As far as the second aspect, that is, the leader of the resistance movement, is concerned, that is correct. That was contained in the statement which Mr. Brown was present at of the -- in 2000. As far as the first is concerned, Your Honours, that is incorrect, because it's not contained in this statement; it's contained in a later statement at which Mr. Brown was not present when it was taken. And accurately he confirmed that he had sent information not to the other side in terms of the opposing army or anything like that, but to Muharem Krzic - which is a different matter - who was the leader of the SDA in Banja Luka. And the implication, of course, Your Honour, was that, particularly in the context of the removal of Muslims from the military, that they were passing information to the other military side. So, Your Honours, that's all that I want to say. But I am saying that when propositions are put, they cannot be summarised like this but they must be put in an accurate fashion. And particularly here where, as I say, the implication was that Mr. Brown personally heard Mr. Selak say that -- Colonel Selak say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, very briefly. I'm sorry I wasn't aware that Mr. Brown was not present at the -- at the time when Mr. Selak was giving his second statement. However, he was an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor. That is why I took the inference that he was informed about that. But, in any case, it wasn't meant to suggest anything else but the facts which Osman Selak stated in his statements, Your Honours. I mean, if I -- if I made a mistake, I am really sorry about that, and I will try to avoid making such mistakes in the future. But I think this was -- this was fairly understandable, at least from my point of view, that he was aware what Osman Selak was talking about in all his statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, two more things. I missed to offer one document which the witness commented upon, that's tab 153. It's document 1D04-9459. It's the -- it's the order of 30th of September, 1992, signed by Naser Oric, which the witness commented. And if there is no opposition, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not altogether clear at the moment from anything that's been said by the witness as to how this is relevant. It was preceded by the assertion that Naser Oric's forces massacred the people here, this well-known event, and, of course, Naser Oric was tried and acquitted of this particular charge, it's fair to say. But if Mr. Zecevic can explain why it's relevant, then I'm perfectly prepared to not object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I produced this document as the reason why the Directive 4 was issued and subsequently the document which is P1789 -- 779, the order to Drina Brigade. And I asked the witness whether he agrees with that proposition, and he agreed with that proposition. That is the only reason why I introduced this document. And I must remind the Trial Chamber that I considered the Directive 4 to be irrelevant and it was admitted. Therefore, I think we are entitled to show the context of how the -- how it came about to this Directive 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, despite the fact I don't think at the moment there is any evidence linking them, I accept that it could be said to be relevant to the context, and therefore I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the last thing is I promised --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. This will become Exhibit 1D402, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I promised that I could be able to give assessment of time needed for cross-examination. I'm afraid, Your Honours, I have three more issues that I would like to discuss with the witness, and I'm pretty certain that I might need two sessions tomorrow. Because of the number of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have been warned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the witness back on the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what about -- perhaps I missed it, but what about the document under tab 3 in your list?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's part of the law library.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's fully translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the law library is stipulated, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hope you're not tired, Mr. Brown. One hour remains today, and I know that these things are not easy. Not easy for me either. Mr. Brown, during your direct examination, page 18691 to 692, you spoke with my learned colleague Ms. Korner about document P1783, which is tab number 15 in the Prosecution binder. I will remind you that this is an order coming from the command of the 30th Partizan Brigade, dated the 31st of May, 1992, entitled, "Formation of the Defence of Kljuc." Do you remember that you commented this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, let me remind you that at the page 18692 you said that that's a unique document, that a defence of Kljuc was mentioned there, and for you this made it an unusual document. I think I'm paraphrasing you here.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, maybe it's the phrase "defence command" was a phrase that I hadn't heard before. And this is a document from the -- a subordinate unit of the corps. So, again, it's -- it was a little bit unusual in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us then analyse this, through the footnote contained in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1D365, can we have this document? That's tab 1 in the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document from 1991, dated the 25th of November, and it's instruction on conducting the civilian affairs in the crisis areas. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know of this document until it was in the binder. It's not a document, I don't think, I've referenced in my report, and it wasn't one that I -- I'd seen until it was placed in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to apologise. I thought that all the documents contained in the binder, the Prosecution binder, are the documents contained in your footnotes, the documents that you analysed. Did you maybe during the proofing see that document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to check my footnotes again, but I don't think this is one that's referenced in my report. I think this week was the first week I'd seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can confirm he -- I showed this to Mr. Brown when he was -- when I spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, bearing in mind that you saw this document, I would like you to take a look at the third page of the document titled, "Tasks of the Civilian Affairs Organs in the Command of the JNA Units and Command of Settlements."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see item number 7? One of the tasks mentioned here by Major General Milan Pujic, deputy secretary for National Defence, is: "In case the civilian government fails to function, ensure the necessary conditions within the JNA units' command, that is, the town command for the forming and the functioning of the organs of civilian government and other organs and bodies." When he mentions town commands, town is a rather more loosely defined term than a city or a settlement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, a town, I'm assuming, is not a city; smaller than a city, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that these instructions, dating from November 1991 defining the tasks of the organs and units in charge of civilian affairs, that they had envisaged the possibility of the establishment of the command of a settlement, which includes also a town command.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, reading this document, it authorises a particular staff function, which is the civilian affairs command. I think I mentioned there was often an officer appointed to civilian affairs within a staff of a formation. This would seem to give tasks to that staff branch, and that if, when a civilian government isn't functioning in an area that the JNA are to be operating, that one of the roles of this branch within the command is to ensure conditions that civilian authorities can function. So whether it relates to -- in an area where there is no civilian authority, that the JNA are to -- a staff branch is to assume that function. Based on the date of the document, it probably is relating to operations in Croatia and what they're expecting to do in Croatia, and I believe that the possible context behind this was that when the JNA conducted operations in Croatia at this time, they were expecting -- their goal, in essence, was to try and get Croatia -- I mean their role was to try and get up to the Hungarian border, in essence to bring Croatia back into Yugoslavia, I assume. And so maybe they felt that one of the functions in that operation would have been that territories would not have had a friendly or a functioning civilian government, and maybe this was a -- relating to that. But town command is not one that I've seen regularly reported through documents, I think as I said previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you would allow for the possibility that this instruction may be linked with the document that - we looked at it a little while ago, P1783 - which was the order by the command of the 30th Partizan Division to mount the Defence of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say it was linked. And in fact, in relation to the defence command, I believe than in the Kljuc Crisis Staff minutes of a couple of days prior to this document it was accepted and agreed that defence command should be established. So this document, I believe, is linked to the decision of the Crisis Staff in Kljuc a few days prior to this. And the Crisis Staff of Kljuc consisted of commanders from subordinate formations of this command, police, and the civilian authorities of Kljuc. So I suspect what happened with this document was that a decision was made at the Kljuc Crisis Staff and agreed that a defence command should be formed and that what fell from this was this more formalised document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll definitely have to show you some other documents now in order to show you that your chain of reasoning is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 886, which is tab 152 in the Defence binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is, again, an order by another brigade, by a command of another brigade, 19th Partizan Brigade, dated 13th of June, 1992, and it relates to Skender Vakuf, which is also within the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, at least that was the situation at the time. No, I didn't mean Skender, I meant Donji Vakuf. And in item number 1, you can see that Defence command for the town of Donji Vakuf is being established. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But certainly this document too refers to the establishment of the command of the town defence, just as in the document that we saw about Kljuc; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to make reference to a defence command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at page 4 of this document. I believe it's very telling, what it says. The last page. The signature is that of the commander, Colonel Branislav Grujic and Captain 1st Class Rade Radic, who confirms the authenticity of the signature. I believe that the correct page in English is the one before this. Item 5 shows that Lieutenant-Colonel Branislav Grujic, the commander of the brigade, appoints the commander of the public security station and that is one Sefulo Sisic, Captain 1st Class. And then Jovo Satara, deputy commander of the public security station and one Srdjan - I can't read his last name - assistant commander of the public security station. In this case, then, the commander, Branislav Grujic, who commands the 19th Brigade, appoints Captain 1st Class, in other words, a member of the army, he commands -- he appoints him commander of the Donji Vakuf Public Security Station; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem so from this document. I don't know whether there had been some agreement prior to this or discussions prior to this or what had happened before, but at face value from this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Unless there are objections, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D403, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you some more documents, sir, much like this one. But let me ask you something before that. From your analytical review of the documents about the 1st Krajina Corps and its military operations, are you familiar with the name of a Colonel Lisica who was the commander of the Doboj operations group?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the name, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Slavko Lisica. I'll show you of those documents. 1D00-2304. The document is dated 29 August 1992. And that's tab 76 in the Defence binder. Here, this Mr. Lisica, in the first paragraph, refers to the instruction we have just discussed. He says: "On the basis of instructions on the work of organs of civilian affairs in times of combat operations and of demonstrated need, I hereby issue the following order ..." Then he says: "The Derventa town command from today on shall only deal with military issues, while all civilian matters shall be transferred to the civilian authorities."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well then, Mr. Brown, this document, in its first paragraph, as I said, states that it was issued on the basis of instructions on the work of organs of civilian affairs in times of combat operations and if demonstrated need. This certainly refers to document 1D365, which I showed you a little earlier and which is under tab 1 of the Prosecution. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the VRS issued their own instructions for the organs of civilian affairs. It may well have been that the VRS in its regulations, bearing in mind this is late 1992, or whether they took existing regulations from the JNA; but they are obviously making reference to some document about the organ of civilian affairs in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I accept that. Here, the commander, Colonel Slavko Lisica, orders that the town command of Derventa from that day on, which is in late August 1992, shall deal only with military issues, whereas all civilian matters shall be transferred to the civilian authorities. This clearly means that from the moment Derventa was liberated, which I believe was in June or July 1992, until the end of August the town command of Derventa was in place and functioned, and that within its remit were not only military matters but also civilian matters. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at this document on its own, I assume what might have happened here is that Derventa was taken in Operation Corridor and there wasn't a functioning civilian government initially, bearing in mind it wasn't, I believe, a Serb municipality. And possibly, here, the military were asked to do, as had been noted before, to establish some kind of town command, and then when the civilian authorities were fully established, that the town command basically was handed over to the civilian War Presidency and that the town commander was to become the representative on the War Presidency in Derventa. And I am assuming that the town command may have been established because the military took that area in Operation Corridor 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mostly agree with your explanation. The essence is that in this document too, which is linked to some instruction on the work of civilian organs, the notion of town command is mentioned. That was actually the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it references town command. I mean, the reference you showed me from Donji Vakuf may have been a similar situation. I know that Donji Vakuf was a very tense municipality. It was right on the border and there was a lot of combat activity. And if I'm not wrong, I think the municipality was split, and there were -- there was a lot of -- I'd have to remind myself, I think, but it was a municipality that saw quite a lot of combat operations. And it may well have been that the reference you had beforehand was a similar sort of position, where there wasn't a functioning government and that the town command may have been established there. But, again, I'm not an expert on the situation in Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, sir, isn't it, that in your work, under 2.215, you deal with a similar situation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, the reference again, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 2.215. And the last sentence reads: "The following weeks in the Posavina were terminated by the establishment of military authority in Odzak municipality." That's a similar situation as the one in Derventa, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D404, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us now make use of the time left today and deal with another topic that you spoke about on examination-in-chief, on page 18702 and the following pages, that is, the issue of paramilitaries. You dealt with that issue from 2.57 through 2.72 of your analysis. And you commented on paramilitaries for the first time when you were analysing combat readiness, which is document P1781. If you remember, there the military says that some groups have sprung into being, some paramilitary groups, whose goals in the war were sometimes contrary to those of the VRS. Do you remember that section of the analysis of combat readiness in 1993?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at document P591, which is tab 36 in the Prosecution binder. And you refer to it in some footnotes, namely footnotes 368 and 382 in your analysis. That's an information -- that's a report on paramilitary formations in the territory of the Serbian Republic; it's dated 28 July 1992. And among others, various groups you commented upon were that the Prosecutor are mentioned here. On page 3 of this document, mention is made of a certain paramilitary group in Zvornik municipality. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the one in the area of Zvornik? "Things have reached ..." That reference there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Here in this document we see, in the last-but-one paragraph in Serbian, on the fourth from the bottom in English, it says: "In the area of Zvornik, things have even reached the stage where an illegal TO staff, which has some paramilitary units under its command, demands that a Zvornik brigade of the army be placed under their command." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if you remember from the analysis of combat readiness where the security administration mentions an arrest operation conducted in cooperation with the bodies of the Ministry of the Interior. It refers to a group that called themselves or were known as the yellow wasps; they were a paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the reference in the document that you're referring to. If you want me to, I can look at it. But I am aware of that group in Zvornik. I don't know the area well and I don't know that organisation, but I know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is enough. On the last page of this document, Zdravko Tolimir, the chief of security of the General Staff of the VRS, gives instructions and orders what shall be done about all these paramilitaries. He says that the paramilitary formations negatively affect the Serbian people in two ways, and then he states the ways. And he adds that every armed Serb in SRBH must be placed under the exclusive command of the army of the SRBH or else he shall be disarmed and legal measures shall be taken. This is an instruction and an order of the chief of security of the General Staff of the VRS, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. After this document, which is dated 28 July 1992, what followed was a document marked P593, tab 38 in the Prosecution binder. And your footnote referring to it is at 373. This is an order of General Talic or, rather, the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, signed by General Talic, I believe, or somebody signed in his stead. It is dated 30 July 1992. And the title is, "Disarmament of Paramilitary Units, Order." You have already commented on this, both in the examination-in-chief and in your report, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if I remember correctly, then you put it in the context of the implementation of the instruction of the chief of security of the Main Staff with regard to the 1st Krajina Corps because that corps, two days after the instruction and the order issued by the chief of security of the Main Staff, issues an order in which he elaborates on the procedure of disarming paramilitaries; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one would seem to follow the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please see page 2. I would like us to comment on items 2 and 3 and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But before that, it says -- or the command says: "To prevent paramilitary organising and placing all units and individuals under the command of the army of the SRBH and pursuant to the Law on the Army and the decision of the Presidency of the SRBH, I order" and then an itemised list follows, 1, 2, 3, et cetera. In paragraph 1, General Talic or, rather, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps gives an option that the paramilitaries shall be offered to integrate into the army, where they can serve in accordance with their military specialty and their skills; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when such formations, which are outside -- which are not under the command of the VRS, should accept the offer to integrate into regular units, they would become part of regular units just as any other soldier, and they would be then -- become parts of a certain corps; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would seem that that's the thrust of both documents, that they are to be integrated into the VRS and if they're integrated, they presumably come under the command of the relevant military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, item 2 includes a limitation, and General Talic says: "Do not include in units individuals and groups which have been involved in crimes and looting or have committed other criminal acts. Disarm and arrest them and bring criminal charges against them" - and now I stress - "in SR BH Army courts, regardless of their citizenship." So, Mr. Brown, it follows from this that General Talic orders that formations that were organised autonomously should be integrated in the VRS but those who have committed crimes should not be integrated but instead disarmed, arrested, and that criminal charges should be pressed against them before military courts. That is, within the framework of the military judiciary of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what is written in his instruction. Whether -- whether that happened or not is another issue, and I think I know of at least, you know, the Milankovic case and the groups from Prijedor that that didn't happen, and then also the issue of the SRBiH courts being used in the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, please, I don't want to go into the details or specific examples. I simply want to have your comment of this order. Whether it was executed in the field and how it was executed in the field is another issue that we are going to visit later. I'm simply now concentrating on the basic meaning of this order, and I would like you to focus on that. Item number 3: "The 1st Krajina Corps orders that the paramilitary formations, groups, and individuals belonging to them who refuse to come under the unified command should be disarmed and arrested in the cooperation with the SRBH MUP and that criminal charges against them should be brought corresponding to the criminal acts that they have committed." So General Talic makes a distinction here between those mentioned in item number 2, who were committing grave offences; for them he orders the military organs to arrest them and disarm them and then give them to the military judiciary. And the others, who committed not so grave offences, among others avoiding the call-up or something like that, and those people he places within the jurisdiction of the police organs. They are supposed to disarm them and initiate criminal proceedings against them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there is an ambiguity in his instruction, but he does at face value say individuals who have been involved in crimes shouldn't be included, yet he allows for the possibility that individuals who have committed crimes can be allowed into the VRS as long as they accept that they should be within the VRS. He almost says in paragraph 3 that, you know, if there are individuals who don't want to be -- bearing in mind, presumably, the previous reference, they're talking about individuals who are known to have committed crimes, there is the possibility, or he allows for the possibility, that individuals who are known to have committed crimes can be included into the VRS as long as they willingly do so. But I do think there is a bit of an ambiguity there because paragraph 2 does say at face value that we're not to let people who are involved in crimes or looting in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to say. In item number 5, Momir Talic, or the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, say: "I forbid the existence of any paramilitary units, groups, and individuals in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. From now on, bring criminal charges against those commanders, competent military territorial organs, and government organs which enable paramilitary organising and avoidance of recruitment and conscription, in accordance with the Law on the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And in item 6 he gives a deadline, the 15th of August, to disarm all paramilitary formations. But the essence of this, Mr. Brown, is as follows: The army's worried about several facets of this situation. First, I agree with you that they worry about the fact that there are some paramilitary formations which are not under their control. Then, as number 2, we can conclude that they are obviously worried also about the fact that these paramilitary formations are committing crimes, and they demand that those crimes be processed. And, as the third item, the army is worried about the fact that certain individuals, by joining the paramilitary formations, avoid their call-up duty as defined by the law, which means that the army doesn't have enough soldiers. They don't have the soldiers who do not respond to the call-up but instead join paramilitary groups who are engaged in criminal activities. Do you agree with my assessment of this order?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, it really -- really is -- it's four -- it's four separate facets. I think it should be broken down, in fairness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, your -- Ms. Korner, I'm sure Mr. Brown is perfectly capable to say, well, I agree with number 1, 2, and do not agree with number 3 and 4, if he does not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try and work through your long question, sir. I would agree that the issue is -- or one of the issues is that they are unhappy that organs are working outside their control. And I would agree that one of the reasons that they do indicate that is because people are, in their eyes, avoiding the call-up. It's not the only reason, I think. There are other reasons. For example, it causes morale problems for soldiers who are on the very front line, when they hear that individuals are behind the front line potentially looting and making money. That was another feature, I think, in some of the reporting. There is another feeling that individuals who are, say, on the front line in the corridor are suffering casualties and having to stay on the fronts line for periods of time when they might perceive others to be behind not really doing their bit. So there are these issues that I also think come into it. I think -- I would accept that in paragraph 2 there is this apparent statement that they are not to have individuals who committed crimes, but my view with the issue of paramilitaries is that they want to have individuals in control under the army to provide manpower and to conduct the operations that they want and it is not about saying that this type of individual is the very last type of individual we want to be giving a weapon and on the front line. They may have had their value in the early stages, but now that we've got an army we want to have them with us. I look at that document and the previous one as -- the undercurrent is that if they come under our control, they will be acceptable, irrespective of what they've done. What this document doesn't say, first and foremost, is: Anybody who has been conducting criminal activities prior to this instruction will, A, be charged, and, B, will find no place in the VRS; it doesn't say that. You know, the document -- paragraph 5 says, I forbid the existence of any paramilitary formations, groups, and individuals in the territory, and -- but from now on bring - from now on bring - criminal charges. Well, they may well have known that there are individuals who fell into that category who have been doing that for months or a period before, but they don't say, We should be charging these people because they have caused problems or have conducted criminal acts. It's saying, From now on if they are going to be doing this, we will charge them. So it was -- my view of this is that this is about getting all individuals in control and under the army, and not necessarily about what they've done previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document, in its item number 2, as you've said, and I'm only going to highlight the key point: Do not include in units such people, instead, arrest them, disarm them, and bring criminal charges against them in army courts. Therefore, item 2 is about the individuals and groups who had committed crimes before that point in time. Sir, in your report, paragraph 2.185, footnote 616, you refer to the document 1D368. It is, at present, marked for identification in this case. This is tab 84 in the Defence binder, and that's a document coming from the Military Prosecutor's Office attached to the Main Staff of the army and which contains the guidelines for the criminal prosecution. You refer to this document when you speak about bringing charges for criminal offences and disciplinary measures in the Army of Republika Srpska. You speak about it in 2.185.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's 84 in the -- in LiveNote. It's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 44. [In English] I'm sorry, my English is getting worse by the minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, it is correct that you referred to this document in your report. And this document of the Military Prosecutor's Office, in short, explains which are the most frequently committed criminal offences and then gives guidelines to the prosecutor's offices about bringing criminal charges against persons who have committed criminal offences; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's been some time since I looked at this, but I think that's what it does deal with.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the expert has used this document in his report, I would now propose to admit it as 1D368 so that it is not only marked for identification any more.

utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I've just looked up, or Mr. Smith's just looked up, I think the objection originally was that there was an assertion that it -- that it was all to do with the war crimes came within the jurisdiction of the Military Prosecutor's Office but otherwise that the witness who was being asked about it wasn't the right witness. utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Your Honours, at this point I'm moving to another issue. Maybe this would be a perfect moment for us to adjourn for today's cross-examination. I'm sure Mr. Brown will appreciate as much as I do your decision in that respect, your favourable decision in that respect. Thank you.
